reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because it promotes a named running event whose stated charitable purpose is supporting children and youth. The invitation to register is presented as participation in that event and accompanied by youth mental-health and charity branding, with no supported promise of investment returns or request for credentials.

citations.quote: RBC Race for the Kids began in 2008 with the first event in New York City.
the money raised for each RBC Race for the Kids event is contributed to charities all over the world that support children and youth.

opening.argument: The closing screen directly pairs a youth-mental-health appeal with “Register today!” and the description directs viewers to sign up online. That frames registration as the action viewers should take to advance a sympathetic cause. Yet these materials do not establish the registration terms, whether payment is required, or how proceeds from this particular event are handled. A careful reviewer should not treat the charitable framing as proof that the solicitation is transparent.

citations.quote: Sign-up and visit us online: https://rbcr4tkottawa.ca/

rebuttal.rebuttal: The stated charitable purpose provides context, but it does not document this event's registration terms or independently verify the implied link between signing up and improving youth mental health. The footage and branding establish an event presentation, not the terms of the solicitation. An external signup invitation paired with a sensitive cause still merits scrutiny.

citations.quote: the money raised for each RBC Race for the Kids event is contributed to charities all over the world that support children and youth.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The opening points to a real registration invitation, but missing terms do not establish deception. The description gives the event's history and states that money raised supports charities for children and youth. The sampled frames show runners, a start line, and event branding, not a reward, payment demand, or false outcome. An external signup link alone is not evidence of a scam.

citations.quote: RBC Race for the Kids began in 2008 with the first event in New York City.
the money raised for each RBC Race for the Kids event is contributed to charities all over the world that support children and youth.

opening.argument: The strongest caution signal is the combination of an urgent-sounding “Register today!” prompt and a link inviting viewers to sign up. The closing screen also ties that action to youth mental health, which can make people less likely to pause and examine the terms. The supplied material does not explain what registration entails or establish how this event's proceeds are handled. Those gaps do not prove fraud, but they mean the charitable appeal and recognizable branding should not be accepted as substitutes for clear, verifiable solicitation details.

citations.quote: Sign-up and visit us online: https://rbcr4tkottawa.ca/

rebuttal.rebuttal: The description's general account of the event's charitable purpose does not answer what a registrant is asked to do or pay for this specific event. Nor does a branded closing screen explain the terms. The appeal, immediate call to register, and online signup route are the relevant solicitation signals; the viewer is given no terms in these supplied materials to assess.

citations.quote: Created as a platform to encourage employee engagement through corporate social responsibility

true_side_reply.rebuttal: “Register today!” is a call to participate in a dated running event, not a promise of easy money or an asset. The closing screen names the event date, and the footage shows a start line and runners. The description identifies a charitable purpose and supplies the signup destination. The absence of detailed terms in this short promotional material does not turn ordinary event promotion into evidence of fraud.

citations.quote: the money raised for each RBC Race for the Kids event is contributed to charities all over the world that support children and youth.
Sign-up and visit us online: https://rbcr4tkottawa.ca/

opening.argument: This is plainly promotional material: the closing screen names the event, urges viewers to register, gives a date, and connects participation to youth mental health. The description also directs viewers to sign up online. That framing steers viewers toward action rather than providing independent scrutiny of the event's arrangements. The supplied evidence does not show the registration terms or verify how this event handles funds, so its charitable presentation should not itself settle whether the solicitation is trustworthy.

citations.quote: Sign-up and visit us online: https://rbcr4tkottawa.ca/

rebuttal.rebuttal: Calling this event promotion does not resolve the concern; promotion is precisely how the material channels viewers toward registration. A broad statement about charities does not disclose this event's signup terms or show how its proceeds are handled. The named cause and event branding may make the invitation appealing, but they are not a substitute for evidence about the transaction being solicited.

citations.quote: the money raised for each RBC Race for the Kids event is contributed to charities all over the world that support children and youth.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The promotional role is consistent with an ordinary charity run: the screen invites registration for a named event on a stated date, while the description explains the event's charitable purpose. The frames show participants running and event signage. The prosecution identifies no false claim, unusual payment, promised reward, or other concrete mechanism that would make this promotion a scam.
